clue.text: It takes pluck to play his part

definitions.text: It takes pluck to play his part

parts.words: It takes pluck to play his part
parts.note: reads as praise for a brave actor, but 'pluck' is plucking strings, so this player's part is plucked on a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: Playing this role needs courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pluck' looks like courage. Here it means plucking strings, and the 'part' is a line of music for an instrument whose strings are plucked.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of the concert instrument with strings plucked by hand performs his part by plucking.

clue.text: It's cast from the heavens

parts.note: 'cast' suggests something thrown down from the sky, but astrologers cast a chart from the positions of the stars

explanation.surface: Something hurled down from the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like thrown; astrologers are said to cast a chart, worked out from the planets and stars.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrologer's chart of the stars at a birth is drawn up, or cast, to predict fortune.

clue.text: This is not intended for quiet reading

definitions.text: This is not intended for quiet reading

parts.words: This is not intended for quiet reading
parts.note: the document read aloud to disperse a crowd is meant to stop a disturbance, so it is never read quietly

explanation.surface: A book too noisy to read in the library.
explanation.walkthrough: The British Riot Act of 1714 was read aloud to order a crowd to disperse; 'to read someone the riot act' is to scold them.
explanation.definitionFit: The proclamation read out loudly to unruly crowds was hardly meant for silent private study.

clue.text: They make improper entries

parts.note: 'entries' looks like bookkeeping, but these are people coming in where they have no right to be

explanation.surface: Dishonest clerks falsifying the ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entries' suggests a ledger; here an entry is going in, uninvited.
explanation.definitionFit: People who barge in where they are not wanted come in without permission, an improper way in.

clue.text: Bath's features. Turner's too

definitions.meaning: a bath has fittings for hot and cold water
a turner (lathe worker) uses tools for cutting screw threads in holes

explanation.surface: A look at the city of Bath as seen in a painter's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath, the English spa city, and Turner, the painter, are misdirections: a bath has water fittings, and a turner on a lathe cuts screw threads with the same-named tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Water outlets fitted to a tub share the name of the threading tools a lathe worker uses.

clue.text: They have no saving grace

parts.note: a saving grace is a redeeming quality, but read literally these people never save: they squander everything

explanation.surface: People with no redeeming quality at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Spendthrifts and idlers who squander money never put anything by, so they lack any gift for saving.

clue.text: Birds seen in the wilds here

definitions.text: Birds seen in the wilds here

indicators.note: the birds are seen inside the other word, set within its letters

parts.note: wilds are wild, uninhabited regions
ernes are sea eagles

explanation.surface: Birds can be spotted out in this remote place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' signals the container; the whole clue also describes the answer, so it is an all-in-one: eagles really are spotted in such places.
explanation.definitionFit: Uninhabited wild country is where wild birds such as eagles are found.

clue.text: One of five we have, naturally

definitions.text: One of five we have, naturally

parts.words: One of five we have, naturally
parts.note: humans naturally have five faculties of perception: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch

explanation.surface: Something we possess five of from birth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five' points to the faculties of sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch are our five natural faculties of perception.

clue.text: The non-latitudinal line

parts.note: the great circle round the Earth has latitude zero, so it is the line with no latitude

explanation.surface: A line that is strict, allowing no latitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latitude' suggests freedom; read geographically, the line at zero degrees latitude has none.
explanation.definitionFit: The great circle midway between the poles lies at zero degrees, so it has no latitude.

clue.text: A foreign gentleman — might be Norse

indicators.note: the letters of Norse might be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A gentleman from abroad, perhaps a Scandinavian.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish title for a man is used as the equivalent of Mr or sir.

clue.text: Where to look for the rest of the poultry

definitions.text: Where to look for the rest of the poultry

parts.words: Where to look for the rest of the poultry
parts.note: 'the rest' looks like the remaining birds, but it means their sleep: where hens perch at night

explanation.surface: A farmer hunting for the remaining chickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The rest of the poultry' seems to mean the other birds; it is their rest, the place they settle to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Hens settle on a perch in the henhouse to sleep, so their resting place is the perch.

clue.text: This litter couldn't be classified as unbearable

definitions.text: This litter couldn't be classified as unbearable

parts.words: This litter couldn't be classified as unbearable
parts.note: 'litter' is a carried couch, and 'unbearable' read literally means unable to be borne by bearers, which a carried litter never is

explanation.surface: This rubbish is not so bad after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' suggests rubbish, and 'unbearable' intolerable; but a litter is a couch carried on poles, and it is made to be borne by bearers.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered couch on poles, carried on bearers' shoulders, is a kind of litter used in Asia.

clue.text: Pygmalion's Galatea, Phase I

parts.note: in the myth the sculptor Pygmalion carved Galatea from ivory before she came to life, so her first phase was carved stone or ivory

explanation.surface: A note on the first stage of a famous mythical woman's life.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed reads 'Phase!'; the page prints 'Phase I'. Pygmalion's Galatea was a carved figure before Venus brought her to life.
explanation.definitionFit: Before coming alive, Galatea was a carved figure, a sculpted likeness standing in Pygmalion's studio.

clue.text: He should know how to handle a pick

definitions.text: He should know how to handle a pick

parts.words: He should know how to handle a pick
parts.note: a pick looks like the digging tool, but it is a choice, as of a sports team, which this person makes

explanation.surface: A labourer who must be skilled with his pickaxe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick' suggests a pickaxe; it is a pick in the sense of a choice, as when a panel chooses a cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who chooses players for a team has to be good at making the right choice.

clue.text: Not out-of-place; exactly the reverse

parts.note: 'out of place' means nowhere fitting; its exact opposite is a word meaning in all places

explanation.surface: Something perfectly fitting rather than out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-place' read as 'in no place' has as its exact opposite 'in all places'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in no place at all is reversed by being in every place.

clue.text: Extravagant bit of accoutrement

indicators.note: only a bit of the word accoutrement is used, a run of letters inside it

explanation.surface: A rather showy piece of a soldier's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Outlandish and eccentric, beyond what is usual, is an extravagant manner or style.

clue.text: Places where there is pressing business afoot

definitions.text: Places where there is pressing business afoot

parts.words: Places where there is pressing business afoot
parts.note: 'pressing business' sounds urgent, but it is grapes being pressed, traditionally trodden by foot

explanation.surface: Offices where urgent work is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressing' means urgent on the surface; here it is the pressing of grapes, and 'afoot' recalls treading them with bare feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapes are grown and pressed for wine on such estates, the plots where vines are cultivated.

clue.text: They should appreciate good tack

parts.note: 'tack' looks like horse gear or tact, but in sailing a tack is a change of course into the wind

explanation.surface: Riders who value well-made saddles and bridles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tack' suggests horse equipment; for sailors a tack is a zigzag course into the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors of pleasure boats change course by tacking, so a well-made tack matters to them.

clue.text: Can't speed make a difference to this performance?

indicators.note: to make a difference to the words is to change their order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering whether dancing faster improves the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a difference to' rearranges CANT SPEED.
explanation.definitionFit: A dance based on steps, such as clog or tap dancing, is a display of footwork.

clue.text: Show business snapshots?

parts.note: reads as photos of entertainers, but each snapshot is an amount of light let onto film, and showing something is laying it open

explanation.surface: Photographs of celebrities in the entertainment world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show business' looks like entertainment; split it as the business of showing, and a snapshot is one frame of film let into the light.
explanation.definitionFit: Each frame of film is a single shot taken, and revealing something publicly is also laying it bare.

clue.text: They can be on hand, or just hanging about, in the theatre

definitions.text: They can be on hand, or just hanging about, in the theatre

parts.words: They can be on hand, or just hanging about, in the theatre
parts.note: 'on hand' means available, but glove figures sit on a hand, and string figures hang from strings on stage

explanation.surface: Stagehands who are ready to help or simply loitering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On hand' and 'hanging about' sound like idle staff; they describe glove figures worn on a hand and string marionettes that dangle.
explanation.definitionFit: Glove figures fit over the hand and marionettes dangle on strings, both performing in shows.

clue.text: Message that disturbs one of Moses' spies

indicators.note: to disturb something is to put it into disorder, so the spy's name is jumbled

parts.note: Caleb was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, in the Book of Numbers

explanation.surface: A news report that upsets one of the Israelite scouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbs' rearranges CALEB, the Biblical spy, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram sent by undersea wire was a common word for a sent communication.

clue.text: One gets the impression they take the rub

definitions.text: One gets the impression they take the rub

parts.words: One gets the impression they take the rub
parts.note: 'the impression' sounds like a feeling, but it is a copy made by rubbing over engraved church memorials

explanation.surface: A suspicion that someone takes the blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the impression' means suspects; here an impression is a rubbing, made by brass rubbing over engraved memorial plates in churches.
explanation.definitionFit: Engraved memorial plates in churches are rubbed with wax on paper to take a copy.

clue.text: Not another name for Inverness

parts.note: an Inverness is a sleeveless cloak with a cape; the clue pretends to rule out a town, while hinting at the garment

explanation.surface: A denial that the Scottish city has a second name.
explanation.walkthrough: Inverness is a Scottish town, but also a cloak with a cape (an Inverness cape). The answer is a South African city whose name contains the cape and a town, but it is not another name for the Scottish one.
explanation.definitionFit: The South African port is a city named after a headland, with town in its name, unconnected to Scotland.

clue.text: Near the end

definitions.meaning: the finish or conclusion of something

explanation.definitionFit: Nearby, adjacent describes the adjective; the noun means a finish or conclusion.

clue.text: It's in brown he looks big

indicators.note: the first word is placed inside the second piece

parts.note: tan is a shade of light brown
the word it, with the apostrophe s read as 'is'

explanation.surface: Someone who seems bigger when dressed in brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container. The definition is a descriptive phrase: a giant of Greek myth is one who looks big.
explanation.definitionFit: A giant of Greek myth, and so any person of great size or stature, looks huge.

clue.text: Yarn of a London street

definitions.meaning: a yarn is a thread, a single twisted fibre
the famous street running from Trafalgar Square towards the City of London

explanation.surface: A tale set in a famous road in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' suggests a story; here it is a thread. The Strand is a major street in central London.
explanation.definitionFit: A single twisted thread of fibre is a length of yarn, and the same name belongs to a busy road near Trafalgar Square.

clue.text: Break free and land on the rocks

indicators.note: to break the word is to smash it apart and reassemble its letters

explanation.surface: A ship's crew escaping and running aground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' rearranges FREE. A ridge of rock just below the sea is solid ground among the rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge of rock or coral at or near the sea's surface forms rocky ground.

clue.text: Open in this place, yonder

parts.note: overt means open, done publicly
here means in this place

explanation.surface: A direction pointing at a spot in the distance.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder is an old word for at a distance, in that direction pointed out.

clue.text: Maternal and filial collaboration in Society

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother, so it stands for the maternal side
filial means of a son or daughter; here the son

explanation.surface: A mother and son working together in a social club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collaboration' joins the two pieces. The definition points to a Freemason, a member of the Masonic Society.
explanation.definitionFit: A Freemason belongs to the brotherhood, a fraternal order called the Society of Freemasons.

clue.text: Inner nature of the French motorist

definitions.meaning: the core quality that makes a thing what it is
a French driver fills up with the French word for petrol

explanation.surface: Describing the true character of a driver from France.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed adds a stray quotation mark the page does not print. In French the word for petrol is the same as the English word for inner nature.
explanation.definitionFit: The fundamental quality of a thing is its heart, and the French for petrol, a driver's fuel, is spelt the same.

clue.text: Subtlety might make sense if dissected

indicators.note: something dissected is cut up and its pieces laid out anew, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Being subtle could help a dissection make more sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The page's 'i!' is 'if': 'dissected' rearranges SENSE IF.
explanation.definitionFit: Delicate skill and refinement in handling things is subtlety in action.
